blocks.instruction: Leia o texto e escolha a alternativa correta. Algumas perguntas pedem inferência — a resposta não está escrita com todas as letras.
blocks.passage:
Supply chain resilience, until recently, was an abstract concept that boards politely listened to and then largely ignored. The last few years changed that permanently. Pandemics, port closures, geopolitical fractures, and the sudden concentration of suppliers in a single region have turned resilience from a talking point into a measurable, costly, strategic priority.

At the heart of resilience is a deceptively simple question: if this link in the chain disappeared tomorrow, what would we do? Strong supply chains have answers ready — alternative suppliers, optional routes, strategic inventory, pre-negotiated contingencies. Fragile ones have only hope.

The trade-off is real and uncomfortable. Resilience is not free. An alternative supplier who only receives a small volume is more expensive per unit; strategic inventory ties up working capital; optionality costs money today against an uncertain benefit tomorrow. Executives who manage this well treat resilience as a portfolio of insurance contracts — bought deliberately, priced honestly, and reviewed regularly. They know the best moment to pay for resilience is long before anybody else values it.

items.q: According to the text, how did boards historically treat supply chain resilience?
options: They listened politely and then largely ignored it
They invested heavily in it every year
They delegated it entirely to logistics teams
They refused to discuss it at all
items.why: "an abstract concept that boards politely listened to and then largely ignored."

items.q: What is the "deceptively simple question" at the heart of resilience?
options: If this link in the chain disappeared tomorrow, what would we do?
How much inventory can we afford to hold?
Which region should we concentrate suppliers in?
items.why: "if this link in the chain disappeared tomorrow, what would we do?"

items.q: The phrase "Fragile ones have only hope" most strongly suggests that…
options: fragile chains are cheaper to run and therefore preferable
fragile chains lack any concrete plan for a disruption
hope is a reasonable substitute for contingencies
resilience cannot be planned in advance
items.why: Inferência: sem alternativas ou contingências, resta apenas torcer — ou seja, nenhum plano real.

items.q: Which statement would the author most likely DISAGREE with?
options: Resilience should be paid for before a crisis makes it obvious
Because resilience is expensive, it is best deferred until a disruption actually occurs
Optionality is a cost incurred today for an uncertain future benefit
Resilience can be managed like a portfolio of insurance contracts
items.why: Inferência: o texto defende justamente pagar cedo — "the best moment to pay for resilience is long before anybody else values it."

items.q: Comparing the author's treatment of resilience to "a portfolio of insurance contracts" implies that resilience is…
options: a one-off purchase that never needs revisiting
a cost deliberately accepted to protect against uncertain risk
something only large companies can afford
items.why: Inferência: seguro é custo assumido de propósito contra risco incerto — comprado deliberadamente e revisado com regularidade.

blocks.instruction: Ouça Oliver apresentando o framework de resiliência ao conselho. Responda sem ler a transcrição — ela só aparece depois de corrigir.

audio.text:
Thank you. The last six weeks have been painful — and I want to use that pain, not waste it. That disruption on the Asian route was not bad luck. It was concentration. Ninety per cent of that component came through a single port, and when that port closed, we had no answer.

Let me be direct about the trade-off, because I don't want anyone leaving this room thinking resilience is free. It isn't. A second supplier, at low volume, costs more per unit. Strategic inventory ties up working capital that finance would rather deploy elsewhere. Optionality is money spent today against a benefit we hope never to need.

But here is how I'd ask you to think about it. Treat these as insurance contracts. You don't buy insurance because you expect the fire; you buy it because the downside is unacceptable. What we just lived through was the fire.

My recommendation is a small, deliberate portfolio: a qualified second source, a modest strategic buffer, and a pre-negotiated alternative route. Priced honestly, reviewed every quarter. The cheapest moment to buy this was two years ago. The second cheapest moment is today.
audio.label: Ouça quantas vezes precisar. A transcrição aparece depois de corrigir.

items.q: What does Oliver identify as the real cause of the six-week disruption?
options: Concentration — ninety per cent of the component came through a single port
A pricing error in the contract
items.why: "That disruption on the Asian route was not bad luck. It was concentration."

items.q: According to Oliver, why does strategic inventory have a cost?
options: It expires quickly and must be replaced
It ties up working capital finance would rather deploy elsewhere
It is taxed at a higher rate
items.why: "Strategic inventory ties up working capital that finance would rather deploy elsewhere."

items.q: Why does Oliver compare resilience measures to buying insurance?
options: Because you buy protection not for the expected case but because the downside is unacceptable
Because they always pay for themselves within a year
Because insurers manage supply chains directly
items.why: "You don't buy insurance because you expect the fire; you buy it because the downside is unacceptable."

items.q: When Oliver says "The cheapest moment to buy this was two years ago. The second cheapest moment is today," he is implying that…
options: the board should wait for prices to fall further
acting now is costly but delaying further only makes it more expensive
the opportunity has already been lost
resilience should be bought only after the next crisis
items.why: Inferência: já que o melhor momento passou, o próximo melhor é agir imediatamente — adiar só encarece.

items.q: How would you best describe Oliver's approach to the board?
options: He downplays the cost to win approval
He is candid about the cost while urging deliberate action
He blames the finance team for the disruption
He recommends doing nothing until the next event
items.why: Inferência: ele é honesto sobre o preço ("resilience is free. It isn't") mas propõe um portfólio pequeno e deliberado — franqueza somada a uma recomendação concreta.

blocks.instruction: O vocabulário da lição aparece aqui em frases novas. Escolha o sentido ou a palavra que cabe no contexto.

items.q: "We keep three months of components as strategic inventory." Strategic inventory is stock held…
options: deliberately as a buffer against disruption
because it was ordered by mistake
only to satisfy an audit requirement
items.why: Estoque estratégico = reserva mantida de propósito para proteger contra rupturas de fornecimento.

items.q: Choose the correct word: "Sourcing everything from one region gives us a dangerous ___ of suppliers."
items.why: Concentration = concentração; depender de uma única região concentra o risco.

items.q: "Maintaining a qualified second supplier gives us optionality." Optionality here means…
options: the freedom to choose an alternative if needed
items.why: Opcionalidade = ter alternativas disponíveis para acionar caso preciso.

items.q: Choose the correct word: "Holding safety stock ___ capital that could otherwise fund growth."
items.why: To tie up capital = imobilizar capital: o dinheiro fica preso no estoque.

items.q: "A fragile supply chain has no plan B." Fragile describes a chain that is…
items.why: Fragile = frágil; quebra com facilidade porque não tem alternativas.

blocks.instruction: Expressões que aparecem em discussões de cadeia de suprimentos. Escolha o sentido no contexto.

items.q: "The board still has to sign off on the resilience budget." To sign off on means to…
items.why: Sign off on = aprovar formalmente, dar o aval.

items.q: "We plan to roll out the second-source strategy market by market." To roll out means to…
items.why: Roll out = implementar de forma progressiva, por etapas.

items.q: "Finance pushed back on the cost of strategic inventory." They…
items.why: Push back on = resistir, contestar — sem necessariamente rejeitar de vez.

items.q: "We identified a second supplier but never followed through on qualifying them." They…
options: failed to see it through to the end
items.why: Follow through = levar até o fim o que foi iniciado; aqui, não foi levado adiante.

items.q: "A modest safety buffer won't move the needle on overall cost." This means it will…
items.why: Move the needle = mexer o ponteiro, causar diferença perceptível.
